Chapter 1: Picturing Distributions with Graphs

The Practice of Statistics in the Life Sciences
by Brigitte Baldi and David S. Moore

Instructor: Ali Raisolsadat

Part I: Exploring Data (The Basics)

1 Chapter 1: Picturing Distributions with Graphs

1.1 What Is Statistics, and Why Should We Study It?

Statistics is the science of learning from data. It gives us a systematic way to collect information, organize it, display it, summarize it, and use it to answer questions.

Statistics is not only a collection of formulas. It is a way of thinking:

What does the data show, what does it not show, and how confident should we be in the conclusion?

This way of thinking is important in the life sciences, but it also appears in chemistry, psychology, economics, business, sports, and modern artificial intelligence.

1.1.1 Statistics Is Everywhere

Consider a few ordinary questions:

  • Biology: Do plants given a fertilizer grow taller than plants that do not receive it?
  • Chemistry: Does changing the catalyst increase the percentage yield of a reaction?
  • Psychology: Do students who sleep longer tend to report better concentration?
  • Economics: Are grocery prices increasing over time, or did one unusually expensive month distort our impression?
  • Artificial Intelligence: If an AI system is trained on a large dataset, does that dataset fairly represent the population where the system will be used?

In every case, the first step is the same: look carefully at the data before trying to make a conclusion.

1.1.2 Why Statistics Still Matters in the Age of AI

Modern AI systems can process enormous amounts of text, images, laboratory measurements, and sensor data. They can also produce tables and graphs almost instantly. But speed does not guarantee that a graph is appropriate or that a conclusion is reasonable.

Statistics helps us ask questions such as:

  • Was the right type of graph used?
  • Is the sample large enough to be informative?
  • Are there unusual observations or possible recording errors?
  • Is an apparent difference large or small?
  • Could the way a graph is drawn exaggerate a pattern?

An AI tool can create a histogram in seconds. You still need statistical reasoning to know whether a histogram is the right graph and how to interpret it.

1.1.3 A First Lesson: Averages Do Not Tell the Whole Story

Both samples in the figure have an average plant height of 20 cm. If we reported only the mean, the samples would appear identical.

The plots reveal something the average hides:

  • Sample A is tightly clustered around 20 cm.
  • Sample B contains much more variation, including plants far below and far above 20 cm.

This is one of the central ideas of introductory statistics:

Numerical summaries are useful, but a graph often reveals structure that a single number cannot.

1.1.4 What We Will Learn in This Chapter

By the end of Chapter 1, you should be able to:

  1. identify individuals and variables in a dataset;
  2. distinguish categorical and quantitative variables;
  3. recognize discrete and continuous quantitative variables;
  4. choose an appropriate bar graph, pie chart, histogram, dotplot, or time plot;
  5. describe a quantitative distribution using SOCS;
  6. identify common ways that graphs can be misleading; and
  7. use graphs to detect possible outliers and data-quality problems.

1.2 Individuals, Variables, and the Structure of Data

1.2.1 Anatomy of a Dataset

Most datasets can be pictured as a table:

  • Rows represent the individuals or cases being studied.
  • Columns represent the variables recorded for those individuals.

Consider a simple plant-growth experiment:

Plant ID Fertilizer Group Germinated? Number of Leaves Height (cm)
P01 None Yes 5 12.4
P02 None Yes 6 13.1
P03 Fertilizer A Yes 8 16.7
P04 Fertilizer A No 0 0.0
P05 Fertilizer B Yes 7 15.9

In this table:

  • the individuals are the individual plants;
  • Fertilizer Group, Germinated?, Number of Leaves, and Height are variables;
  • Plant ID is mainly an identifier used to keep track of each plant.

First question to ask about any dataset: What does one row represent?

1.2.2 Two Fundamental Types of Variables

Once we know the individuals, we classify the variables. The most important first distinction is between categorical and quantitative variables.

1.2.2.1 Categorical Variables

A categorical variable places an individual into a group or category.

Examples include:

  • blood type: A, B, AB, O;
  • fertilizer group: none, A, B;
  • reaction outcome: complete, partial, no reaction;
  • university program: biology, chemistry, psychology, economics.

Categorical variables can be:

  • Nominal: categories have no natural order, such as blood type or treatment group.
  • Ordinal: categories have a meaningful order, such as low, medium, high or poor, fair, good, excellent.

1.2.2.2 Quantitative Variables

A quantitative variable records a numerical amount for which arithmetic is meaningful.

Examples include:

  • plant height in centimeters;
  • reaction time in milliseconds;
  • temperature in degrees Celsius;
  • mass in grams;
  • concentration in mg/L;
  • price in dollars.

A useful check is:

Would taking an average of these numbers have a meaningful interpretation?

If yes, the variable is usually quantitative. If the numbers are only labels, the variable is categorical.

1.2.3 The Coding Trap: Numbers Can Still Be Categories

Suppose a spreadsheet uses

  • 1 = Control,
  • 2 = Fertilizer A,
  • 3 = Fertilizer B.

The variable is still categorical. The numbers are only codes. An average treatment code of 1.8 would not have a useful scientific meaning.

This is why variable type depends on what the values mean, not on whether they are written using digits.

1.2.4 Quantitative Variables: Discrete vs. Continuous

Quantitative variables can be divided further.

1.2.4.1 Discrete Quantitative Variables

A discrete variable usually comes from counting.

Examples:

  • number of leaves on a plant;
  • number of bacterial colonies on a plate;
  • number of customers entering a store;
  • number of incorrect answers on a quiz.

There are gaps between possible values. A plant can have 7 or 8 leaves, but not 7.42 leaves.

1.2.4.2 Continuous Quantitative Variables

A continuous variable usually comes from measuring.

Examples:

  • plant height;
  • body mass;
  • reaction time;
  • temperature;
  • pH;
  • concentration.

A measurement can, in principle, take many values between two recorded values. A scale might display 15.2 g, but a more precise instrument could report 15.23 g or 15.231 g.

1.2.5 Count or Measure? A Simple Rule

Question Usually Produces Example
How many? Discrete quantitative Number of leaves
How much? Continuous quantitative Plant mass
Which group? Categorical Fertilizer type
What level or rating? Ordinal categorical Low / Medium / High

This rule is not perfect in every advanced application, but it is a very useful starting point for introductory statistics.

1.2.6 From Variable Type to Graph Type

The variable type helps determine the graph:

Situation Good Starting Graph Main Question
One categorical variable Bar graph Which categories are most or least common?
Simple parts of one whole Pie chart How is one whole divided?
One quantitative variable, small sample Dotplot What are the individual values and overall pattern?
One quantitative variable, larger sample Histogram What is the shape of the distribution?
Measurements recorded over time Time plot Is there a trend, cycle, or sudden change?

This table is a starting point. The best graph also depends on the question you are trying to answer.

1.3 Categorical Variables: Frequency Tables and Bar Graphs

1.3.1 The Distribution of a Categorical Variable

The distribution of a variable describes the values the variable takes and how often those values occur.

For a categorical variable, we commonly summarize the distribution with:

  • Frequency (count): number of observations in each category;
  • Relative frequency (proportion): count divided by the total sample size;
  • Percentage: proportion multiplied by 100%.

If 18 of 40 students choose biology as their preferred science elective, then

\[ \text{Proportion choosing biology}=\frac{18}{40}=0.45, \]

so 45% chose biology.

1.3.2 Example 1.1: Reaction Outcomes in a Chemistry Lab

Suppose 50 reaction trials are classified as follows:

Reaction Outcome Count Percentage
Complete reaction 28 56%
Partial reaction 15 30%
No visible reaction 7 14%
Total 50 100%

A frequency table is useful when we want exact values. A graph is useful when we want the pattern to be visible immediately.

1.3.3 Bar Graphs: The Default Choice for Categorical Data

A bar graph represents each category with a separate bar. The height of the bar represents a count, proportion, or percentage.

1.3.3.1 When to Use a Bar Graph

Use a bar graph when:

  • the variable is categorical;
  • you want to compare category sizes;
  • you are comparing percentages across different groups; or
  • you want readers to see small differences clearly.

1.3.3.2 How to Read a Bar Graph

When describing a bar graph, ask:

  1. Which category is largest?
  2. Which category is smallest?
  3. Are any categories similar in size?
  4. Are the vertical axis and units clearly labeled?
  5. Are the values counts or percentages?

Important: Bars are separated because the categories are distinct.

1.3.4 Pie Charts: Parts of One Whole

A pie chart divides one whole into slices. It can be appropriate when:

  • all categories belong to the same group;
  • the categories are mutually exclusive;
  • the categories account for the entire whole; and
  • there are only a few categories.

Both displays show the same blood-type percentages. The pie chart makes the part-to-whole idea clear, but the bar graph makes comparisons easier—especially the difference between the smaller categories.

1.3.4.1 Bar Graph or Pie Chart?

For most scientific work, a bar graph is the safer default because people compare lengths along a common scale more easily than angles or areas.

Use a pie chart only when the part-to-whole relationship itself is the main message.

1.4 Choosing the Wrong Graph: What Can Go Wrong?

A graph can be technically polished and still communicate the data poorly. Statistics is not only about creating graphs; it is also about judging whether a graph is appropriate and fair.

1.4.1 Mistake 1: Using a Line Graph for Nominal Categories

Blood type is a nominal categorical variable. There is no meaningful numerical path from O to A to B to AB.

The line graph connects the categories as if movement between adjacent categories has a continuous meaning. The bar graph avoids that false suggestion.

Rule: Use lines when order or continuity matters—especially time—not simply because a software package offers a line-chart button.

1.4.2 Mistake 2: Truncating the Vertical Axis of a Bar Graph

Catalyst A has an average reaction yield of 78%, while Catalyst B has an average yield of 82%. The actual difference is 4 percentage points.

In the right-hand graph, the vertical axis begins near 75%. Because bar length represents magnitude, the difference appears far more dramatic than it really is.

For ordinary bar graphs, the vertical axis should usually begin at zero.

A nonzero baseline is sometimes useful for other graph types, but when bars encode magnitude by length, truncation can strongly exaggerate differences.

1.4.3 Mistake 3: Making a Pie Chart from Percentages with Different Denominators

Suppose 72% of first-year students, 65% of second-year students, 61% of third-year students, and 58% of fourth-year students report sleeping at least seven hours per night.

These percentages come from four different groups. They are not four pieces of a single whole. Turning them into a pie chart creates a fake 100% total that has no meaningful interpretation.

Use a bar graph to compare rates across groups.

1.4.4 A Quick Fair-Graph Checklist

Before trusting a graph, ask:

  • Does the graph type match the variable type?
  • Are the axes clearly labeled?
  • Are units shown?
  • Does a bar graph begin at zero?
  • Are percentages using the same denominator?
  • Is anything important hidden by the scale, bin width, or ordering?
  • Does the title describe the data without exaggerating the conclusion?

1.5 Quantitative Variables: Histograms and Distributions

1.5.1 From Individual Measurements to a Distribution

Quantitative data often contain many distinct values. If 150 plants have heights such as 17.8 cm, 18.1 cm, 18.3 cm, 18.4 cm, and so on, a separate bar for every exact height would be difficult to read.

A histogram solves this problem by grouping nearby numerical values into intervals called bins or classes.

1.5.2 Anatomy of a Histogram

A histogram:

  1. divides the numerical scale into intervals;
  2. counts how many observations fall in each interval; and
  3. draws touching bars to show those frequencies.

Histogram bars touch because the horizontal axis is numerical and continuous.

This is one of the easiest ways to distinguish a histogram from a bar graph.

1.5.3 Bar Graph vs. Histogram

Feature Bar Graph Histogram
Variable type Categorical Quantitative
Horizontal axis Category labels Numerical intervals
Bars Separated Touching
Order May be rearranged for nominal categories Must follow numerical order
Main purpose Compare categories Show the shape of a distribution

1.5.4 Example 1.2: Body Lengths of 44 Great White Sharks

Marine biologists measured the body lengths of 44 great white sharks, in feet:

\(18.7 \quad 12.3 \quad 18.6 \quad 16.4 \quad 15.7 \quad 18.3 \quad 14.6 \quad 15.8 \quad 14.9 \quad 17.6 \quad 12.1\)
\(16.4 \quad 16.7 \quad 17.8 \quad 16.2 \quad 12.6 \quad 17.8 \quad 13.8 \quad 12.2 \quad 15.2 \quad 14.7 \quad 12.4\)
\(13.2 \quad 15.8 \quad 14.3 \quad 16.6 \quad 9.4 \quad 18.2 \quad 13.2 \quad 13.6 \quad 15.3 \quad 16.1 \quad 13.5\)
\(19.1 \quad 16.2 \quad 22.8 \quad 16.8 \quad 13.6 \quad 13.2 \quad 15.7 \quad 19.7 \quad 18.7 \quad 13.2 \quad 16.8\)

A possible frequency table using 2-foot classes is:

Length Class (feet) Count Approx. Percentage
9.1 to 11.0 1 2%
11.1 to 13.0 5 11%
13.1 to 15.0 12 27%
15.1 to 17.0 15 34%
17.1 to 19.0 8 18%
19.1 to 21.0 2 5%
21.1 to 23.0 1 2%
Total 44 99%*

The percentages total 99% because of rounding.

Both histograms use the same 44 measurements. The overall pattern is similar, but the details change when we change the bin width.

1.5.5 The Bin-Width Problem

The choice of bin width can strongly affect the appearance of a histogram:

  • Too few bins: important features are smoothed away.
  • Too many bins: random sampling noise can look like a meaningful pattern.
  • Reasonable bin width: shows the overall structure without hiding or exaggerating detail.

There is no single perfect number of bins for every dataset. A good practice is to inspect a few reasonable choices and check whether the main interpretation stays similar.

A histogram should help reveal the data—not manufacture a story.

1.6 Describing Quantitative Distributions: SOCS

Once a quantitative variable has been graphed, we need a consistent way to describe what we see.

Use SOCS:

  • S — Shape
  • O — Outliers
  • C — Center
  • S — Spread

1.6.1 Shape

Common shapes include:

  • symmetric: the two sides are roughly mirror images;
  • skewed right: the longer tail extends toward larger values;
  • skewed left: the longer tail extends toward smaller values;
  • unimodal: one main peak;
  • bimodal: two main peaks.

The seed-germination distribution is right-skewed: many seeds germinate relatively early, while a smaller number take much longer.

Skewness is named for the direction of the long tail, not the location of the tallest bar.

1.6.2 Outliers

An outlier is an observation that falls far from the overall pattern.

An unusual value is not automatically an error. It could be:

  • a genuine extreme observation;
  • a data-entry mistake;
  • a measurement problem; or
  • an observation from a different population.

Do not remove an observation simply because it looks unusual. Investigate it first.

1.6.3 Center

The center describes a typical or middle value in the distribution.

In this chapter, you may estimate the center visually. In the next chapter, we will calculate numerical measures such as the mean and median.

1.6.4 Spread

The spread describes how variable the data are.

A distribution where values are tightly packed has small spread. A distribution extending over a wide range has large spread.

The opening example in this chapter showed why spread matters: two datasets can have the same mean but very different variability.

1.6.5 Writing a Good SOCS Description

A good description should use the variable name and units.

Instead of writing:

Right-skewed with one outlier.

write something like:

The distribution of seed germination times is unimodal and right-skewed. Most seeds germinated within the first several days, while a small number took much longer. The distribution is centered around a few days and has a long right tail.

The second description explains the graph in context.

1.6.6 Example 1.3: SOCS for Shark Lengths

Using the shark histogram:

  • Shape: roughly unimodal and fairly symmetric through the center;
  • Outliers: the smallest shark at 9.4 ft and largest at 22.8 ft appear separated from much of the data;
  • Center: approximately 15–16 ft;
  • Spread: from 9.4 ft to 22.8 ft.

At this stage, the goal is not to calculate every summary exactly. The goal is to learn how to read the distribution.

1.7 Dotplots: Showing Individual Values

1.7.1 Why Use a Dotplot?

A histogram groups values into bins, so the exact observations are hidden. For a small dataset, we often want to see every value.

A dotplot places one dot for each observation above a numerical scale.

Use a dotplot when:

  • the sample is small or moderate;
  • individual values matter;
  • repeated values are useful to see; or
  • you want a simple comparison between small groups.

1.7.2 How to Read a Dotplot

Look for the same features as in a histogram:

  • clusters;
  • gaps;
  • center;
  • spread;
  • unusual observations.

The advantage is that the raw observations remain visible.

1.7.3 Example 1.4: Plant Height With and Without Fertilizer

Each dot represents one plant.

From the graph we can say:

  • the fertilizer group tends to have larger plant heights;
  • the two groups still overlap;
  • the fertilizer group appears shifted somewhat to the right;
  • no single observation is extremely separated from the rest.

Notice the wording: the graph shows a difference in the observed samples. A graph alone does not prove that the same difference must occur in every future plant.

1.7.4 Dotplot vs. Histogram

Dotplot Histogram
Shows individual observations Groups observations into bins
Excellent for small samples Excellent for larger samples
Repeated values can be seen Overall shape is easier to see when data are dense
Easy to count the sample size Exact values are not visible

There is no strict cutoff such as “30 observations means histogram.” The choice depends on how readable the individual points remain.

1.8 Time Plots: When Order Matters

1.8.1 Why Time Needs Its Own Graph

A histogram or dotplot tells us what values occurred. It does not tell us when they occurred.

When measurements are collected in chronological order, that order may contain the most important information.

Examples include:

  • temperature measured every hour;
  • bacterial growth recorded every 30 minutes;
  • monthly unemployment rates;
  • daily chemical calibration measurements;
  • annual rainfall.

A time plot places time on the horizontal axis and the measured variable on the vertical axis.

1.8.2 What to Look for in a Time Plot

Look for:

  • trend: a long-term upward or downward movement;
  • cycle: a repeating pattern;
  • sudden change: an abrupt jump or drop;
  • unusual observation: a point that does not fit nearby values.

1.8.3 Example 1.5: A Repeating Daily Pattern

The measurements rise and fall in a repeating pattern over approximately 24 hours. A histogram of the same temperatures could show their overall distribution, but it would hide the repeating cycle.

1.8.4 Example 1.6: A Histogram Can Hide Instrument Drift

The two panels contain the same measurements.

  • The histogram shows which concentration values occurred most often.
  • The time plot reveals that the measured concentration gradually increases over the 60 days.

If the sample is supposed to be a constant 100 mg/L calibration standard, the time plot raises an important data-quality question: is the instrument slowly drifting?

This example illustrates a general rule:

When time order is meaningful, plot the data against time before ignoring the order.

1.9 Outliers and Data Quality

1.9.1 Always Investigate Unusual Values

When you see an outlier or sudden spike, ask:

  1. Was the value entered correctly?
  2. Are the units correct?
  3. Was the instrument working correctly?
  4. Is the value scientifically plausible?
  5. Could it be a genuine but unusual observation?

1.9.2 Example 1.7: A Data-Entry Error

Most recorded temperatures are near 37°C, but one value is 370°C. The graph makes the problem obvious immediately.

Without plotting the data first, that value could distort later numerical summaries.

1.9.3 Common Data Problems That Graphs Can Reveal

Problem Example What You Might See
Typing error 19.4 entered as 194 One extreme observation
Wrong unit Some masses entered in mg instead of g Two separated groups or an extreme gap
Missing-value code Missing recorded as -99 A strange stack of values at -99
Instrument drift Calibration slowly changes over days Gradual trend in a time plot
Duplicated record Same row copied twice Repeated or unusually stacked points

Graphs are not only for presentation. They are also tools for checking the quality of the data.

1.10 Practice: Matching Questions to Variables and Graphs

1.10.1 Apply Your Knowledge 1.1: Breakfast Cereals

Consider a dataset describing 77 breakfast cereals:

Brand Manufacturer Type Calories Sugar (g)
All Bran K C 70 5
All Bran Fiber K C 50 0
Almond Delight R C 110 8
Apple Cheerios G C 110 10
Apple Jacks K C 110 14

Questions

  1. What are the individuals?
  2. Which variables are categorical?
  3. Which variables are quantitative?
  4. Which graph would you use to display Manufacturer?
  5. Which graph would you use to display Sugar for all 77 cereals?

Answers

  1. The individuals are the 77 cereal brands.
  2. Manufacturer and Type are categorical.
  3. Calories and Sugar are quantitative.
  4. A bar graph is appropriate for Manufacturer.
  5. A histogram is a good starting graph for Sugar because it is quantitative and the dataset is large enough to focus on the overall distribution.

1.10.2 Apply Your Knowledge 1.2: Choosing the Graph

Choose the best graph for each situation.

Question Variable / Structure Best Starting Graph
Which blood type is most common in a sample? Categorical Bar graph
How are four categories divided within one whole? Categorical, part-to-whole Pie chart or bar graph
What is the distribution of 150 plant heights? Quantitative Histogram
What are the exact reaction times of 12 participants? Quantitative, small sample Dotplot
Is river temperature changing throughout the day? Quantitative over time Time plot

1.10.3 A Five-Step Approach for Exam Questions

When you are given a new dataset or graph-selection question:

  1. Identify the individual: What does one row represent?
  2. Identify the variable: What characteristic was recorded?
  3. Classify the variable: Categorical or quantitative? If quantitative, discrete or continuous?
  4. Ask whether time order matters.
  5. Choose the graph that answers the question most clearly.

1.11 Master Guide: Which Graph Should You Use?

Data Situation Recommended Graph What to Describe Common Mistake
Categorical counts or percentages Bar graph Largest/smallest categories, comparisons Connecting categories with a line
Parts of one whole Pie chart Dominant slices, part-to-whole structure Using separate group percentages as slices
Small quantitative sample Dotplot Individual values, clusters, gaps, SOCS Hiding a tiny sample inside histogram bins
Larger quantitative sample Histogram SOCS and overall shape Choosing bins that hide or exaggerate patterns
Data recorded over time Time plot Trend, cycles, sudden changes Ignoring the time order

1.11.1 What Should You Say When Describing a Graph?

1.11.1.1 For a Bar Graph

  • identify the most and least common categories;
  • compare important percentages or counts;
  • mention the sample or denominator when relevant.

1.11.1.2 For a Histogram or Dotplot

Use SOCS:

  • Shape
  • Outliers
  • Center
  • Spread

1.11.1.3 For a Time Plot

Describe:

  • trend;
  • cycles;
  • sudden changes;
  • unusual observations.

1.12 Key Terminology Review

  • Statistics: The science of learning from data.
  • Individual (Case): The object or person represented by one observational unit in the dataset.
  • Variable: A characteristic recorded for an individual.
  • Categorical Variable: Places observations into groups or categories.
  • Quantitative Variable: Records a numerical amount.
  • Discrete Variable: A quantitative variable that usually results from counting.
  • Continuous Variable: A quantitative variable that usually results from measuring.
  • Distribution: The values a variable takes and how often those values occur.
  • Bar Graph: A graph for categorical data with separated bars.
  • Pie Chart: A part-to-whole display for one categorical variable.
  • Histogram: A graph for quantitative data using touching bins.
  • Dotplot: A graph showing individual quantitative observations as dots.
  • Time Plot: A graph of a variable against chronological time.
  • SOCS: Shape, Outliers, Center, Spread.
  • Outlier: An observation that lies far from the overall pattern.
  • Trend: A long-term upward or downward movement over time.
  • Cycle: A pattern that repeats over time.

1.13 Chapter 1 Summary

The main goal of this chapter is not to memorize graph names. It is to learn to match the graph to the data and the question.

1.13.1 The Core Rules

  1. Know what one row represents. Identify the individuals before analyzing variables.
  2. Classify the variable. Categorical and quantitative variables require different displays.
  3. Use bar graphs for categorical comparisons. Use pie charts only for simple parts of one whole.
  4. Use histograms to see the shape of larger quantitative datasets. Check whether the bin width changes the story.
  5. Use dotplots when individual numerical values are still readable.
  6. Use time plots when order matters. A histogram can hide a trend or cycle.
  7. Describe quantitative distributions using SOCS.
  8. Do not trust a graph automatically. Check axes, scales, denominators, labels, and design choices.
  9. Plot data before calculating summaries. Graphs can reveal errors and unusual observations immediately.

1.13.2 Final Graph Checklist

Before interpreting or presenting a graph, ask:

  • What are the individuals?
  • What variable is being displayed?
  • Is the variable categorical or quantitative?
  • Does time order matter?
  • Is this the right graph for the variable?
  • Are the title, axes, and units clear?
  • Could the scale or binning exaggerate or hide a pattern?
  • What is the main pattern visible in the data?

1.13.3 What’s Next? Chapter 2 — Describing Distributions with Numbers

In Chapter 1, we learned to see center and spread. In Chapter 2, we will learn to calculate them.

We will introduce numerical summaries such as:

\[ \text{Mean} \qquad \text{Median} \]

and measures of variability such as:

\[ \text{Range} \qquad \text{Interquartile Range} \qquad \text{Standard Deviation}. \]

The key idea will remain the same: numbers and graphs should support each other.
